title: The frontend accepts x * 2.0 and refuses 2.0 * x, and two of eleven DCU campaigns lost their candidate to it
backend: all backends; the rule is in the shared frontend
target: all declared targets; observed on gfx938
executor_revision: none: the refusal is at construction, before any device

evidence.retained: bw1100 campaign evidence for rmsnorm-20260917-181121 and gelu_tanh-20260917-210609, each carrying a candidate_rejected event with this diagnostic; eleven DCU campaigns on 2026-09-17 were read together to pool the refusals
sites: src/open_cake_ir/compiler/frontend.py:437-439 -- a literal is admitted only at position 1, for any operator
measured through cake.parse: `t * 2.0` and `t + 1.0` accepted, `2.0 * t` and `1.0 + t` refused with this message

observation:
The rule admits a literal only as the second operand, and it applies to every operator rather than to the ones where operand order carries meaning. Measured through the public frontend: `t * 2.0` parses, `2.0 * t` does not; `t + 1.0` parses, `1.0 + t` does not.

For `mul` and `add` the two forms denote the same computation, and `2.0 * x` is how it is written in NumPy and in PyTorch, which is the editing model P1 asks to keep familiar. For `sub` and `div` they do not: `2.0 - x` is not `x - 2.0`, and refusing a leading literal there is a real restriction with a reason behind it. One rule covers both cases and states only the position it wants.

What it costs is visible rather than argued. Pooling the candidate_rejected events across eleven DCU campaigns on one day, this diagnostic accounts for two of them -- rmsnorm and gelu_tanh both lost a candidate to writing a scalar on the left. Both runs recovered and qualified later, so the cost is turns rather than outcomes, but turns are the budget the loop spends.

The pooled set is worth recording beside it, because a single run does not show which refusals recur: `unsupported Schedule operation 'range'` twice, `expected a literal or a previously declared name` twice, `lm.reduce(...).across_loop=true is the historical omitted spelling` twice, `unsupported Schedule operation 'sqrt'` once, and single-assignment once. The IR knows rsqrt and not sqrt, which is the one of these that is a missing primitive rather than a spelling the author had to guess.

Added after the fact, from the same pooled reading: softsign refused with `unsupported Schedule operation 'maximum'`. The elementwise vocabulary is add, div, exp, exp2, fma, mul, reciprocal, relu, rsqrt, square, sub and tanh -- no abs, no maximum, no sign, no sqrt. It would be wrong to call softsign inexpressible: |x| is relu(x) + relu(-x), and x / (1 + |x|) written that way parses in seven elementwise operations, which was checked rather than assumed. What the author hit is that the composition is not obvious from a vocabulary list, and the refusal names the operation it rejected without naming what the target does have. That is the same shape as the across_loop diagnostic: a blocking check that says no without saying what would work spends a turn and teaches nothing.

The re-run also shows the limit of a better message. per_channel_moments drew both improved diagnostics in one turn -- the literal one on a non-commutative operator, where the refusal is correct and now names which operators admit a leading literal, and the across_loop one now telling it to omit the field -- and still exhausted its budget at two turns. A refusal arrives after the author has written the thing, so a clearer one buys a better next attempt rather than a first attempt that does not need it.
proposed_change:
Two candidates, and the first is smaller than it looks. Canonicalise a leading literal on the commutative operators -- `mul` and `add` -- to the second position at construction, which is exactly what P3 asks of equivalent spellings, and keep refusing it on `sub` and `div` where order is meaning. The refusal that remains should say which operators admit it rather than stating a position, since an author who reads `only as the second operand` learns nothing about why `x - 2.0` was the form that worked.

That is a Compiler change: it needs the Corpus Gate, a case each way, and the analyses that go with it, which is the shape F-2026-09-17-008 exists to insist on. It is not urgent -- the loop recovers -- and it is cheap, which is the argument for doing it deliberately rather than never.

The `across_loop=true` diagnostic is a separate and smaller act: it names what the author wrote as `historical` without naming what to write instead, and a blocking check that does not name the correct form spends a turn teaching the author nothing.

Whether `sqrt`, `abs` or `maximum` should join the elementwise vocabulary is a third question and needs its own evidence. Each is already composable -- sqrt from rsqrt and reciprocal, abs from two relus -- so the case for a primitive rests on whether the composition costs accuracy or instructions on some target, which nothing here measures. The cheaper half of that question needs no IR change at all: a refusal that named the composable alternatives would have cost softsign nothing.
verified_by: tests/contracts/test_python_frontend.py -- the canonicalisation, the refusal that remains on sub and div, and that buffer operands are not reordered; Corpus Gate 155 of 155 and the full suite 2035 passed at that commit. A before/after on the DCU was attempted and does not support an outcome claim: of four tasks that had lost their candidate, cosine_similarity and residual_rmsnorm qualified on the re-run and per_channel_moments and softmax did not. residual_rmsnorm had failed on `sqrt`, which nothing here changed, so run-to-run variance alone produces a conversion at this sample size and cosine_similarity's cannot be attributed to the fix. What is verified is the mechanism, by the tests and by the new messages appearing in retained rejections; what is not verified is that either fix raises the qualification rate
